Switzerland is one of the wealthiest economies in the world. This success surely has many reasons. An important reason is that the Swiss people - unlike, for example, the Germans, Frenchmen and Italians - have refused to participate in socialist experiments in the past. Within its borders, it employs decentralization towards a productive competition of regions. Outside its borders, Switzerland is an open economy. It is very much involved in the international division of labor but at the same time free from coercive intervention from abroad.

The European Union moves in a different direction. It wants to create a thoroughly state-interventionist, centralized construction in which markets are regulated and taxation and regulatory legislation becomes standardized. This is not just about harmonization, but also centralization of power. Irrespective of glaring dysfunctionalities in issues of currency and fiscal policy, the political elite of the EU wants to "finalize the economic and monetary union." They want to do this using "a stronger coordination of economic policy, convergence, and solidarity."

Such an interventionist model of economy and society in the EU cannot work and is economically doomed to fail. The state intervenes in the economy and in society with the promise to do good and to restrict itself to previously defined measures. But the interventions lead to unintended consequences and side effects. Correcting them necessitates further interventions. These will also miss their target and make the situation worse. And it goes on like that. At the end of the intervention spiral, the state is almighty, citizens and companies are subordinates, the economy is half or fully socialist.

The fatal effects of interventionism can be illustrated using the common currency of the Euro. It is a paper money and the continuous expansion of its supply has led to a massive debt pyramid. States and banks, but also consumers and companies can only be spared from a bankruptcy when the European Central Bank sets the interest rates at or below zero and uses its electronic printing press. The economies are addicted to the drug of easy money.

If the ECB decides to move towards "helicopter money", there will be no holding back. Then the ECB council will decide which citizens, companies and states receive how much money at which time. The Euro economies will suddenly be centrally planned. The idea that growth and employment will thrive in such a monetarily planned economy is completely illusory. Without free markets, without free competition, you can neither create nor preserve prosperity. Rather, a regression to a pre-capitalistic epoch happens, in which shortages and poverty are commonplace.

The economic decline of the EU and now also the problems which come from a stream of immigrants to the state community (which is not being wanted by many citizens), the Brits (who are already against the EU) - exactly these EU citizens that enjoy a position of privilege and haven't traded their currency for the Euro - react. On June 23rd 2016 the Brits will vote on whether their country remains in the EU. In advance of the decision, the EU supporters are already working hard and warning the Brits about the allegedly catastrophic consequences of a "Brexit".

For example, British trade with the EU could suffer, as it is being said: Currently the Brits are selling roughly 50 percent of its exports to the EU. Also investments by foreigners in Great Britain could be negatively affected and that could destroy jobs. First and foremost, the financial center of London - an important economic factor for the island state - could lose its attractiveness. But these doubts can be defused.

In a "Brexit" it would be in the interest of the Brits and all EU countries to give the island a "Norway status": Since 1994 and thanks to the European Economic Area, Norway has access to the European single market, but at the same time the country is free from EU mandates such as legislation in agriculture, fishery and law. Alternatively, the Brits could strive for a tight network of free trade agreements like Switzerland did with the EU, especially like the "Bilateral I" agreements (1999).

Concerning the flow of foreign investments, a "Brexit" could be a net positive for Great Britain. Exiting the European Union brings freedom for Britain's economic policy which can be used to improve production - such as by lowering taxes and getting rid of regulations. If Great Britain would receive a Norway or Switzerland status, it would be attractive for foreign investors to invest in it.

That a "Brexit" harms the London financial center is very improbable. Not even the introduction of the Euro could dethrone the financial center of London, just the opposite: The British city has become the financial community #1 worldwide - even being superior to New York. The British capital does not need to fear a migration of banks and talent to Paris, Frankfurt or Rome, if anything, it would fear a migration to New York, Singapore, Hong Kong or Tokyo.

For the EU supporters, a "Brexit" would be a nasty shock. It could encourage other EU members to do the same. A "Brexit" could have the potential to create forces which lead to a dissolving of the EU model of centralization. That which is, of course, a nightmare for the Europe centralizers is a great chance for the citizens and companies: Going back to the model of a competition of regions which fight for the best environment for tax citizens and companies, is then coming closer.

Basically, economic prosperity does not have many requirements. Respecting and protecting property, free markets and free competition are indispensable. Dispensable, even harmful, are all political interventions which want more than that. A British exit from the EU should not be feared, but celebrated as a catalyst for reform. It would be a homage to the Swiss model which has successfully created prosperity through the "appeal of small units" and a high degree of openness towards the world economy. A "Brexit" could be the call that leads Europe back to growth and employment.

The desired exit of a country out of a federation must be regarded as an exercise of its right of self-determination. Cooperation between states must be voluntary and based on mutual gain. Is that no longer the case, then it must be possible to unilaterally cease cooperation. The possibility to exit in case of dissatisfaction - if all negotiations fail - is an effective incentive leading the EU towards a direction which is more inclined to the goals of its citizens.

Thus, a "Brexit" is the key to a better, more free and prosperous Europe. You can have open markets and free movement of labor and capital without a EU power centralization. You just need to remember that Europe's economic success comes not from a central political power but from a decentralized order. #XX Dav

The sites numbers are way down. New registrations, new posts, new visitors, etc, all down significantly on last year. We need to do something about it before it's too late to do anything. The survey in particular had a large number (more than half) of answers across all groups citing our moderation as a problem. It needs a facelift - which is not at all the same thing as suggesting it needs a big change. Some tweaks to how we present things rather than any real need to change the processes are what I'm thinking.

With that in mind, I do have one suggestion I think we can all take on board which should help soften the perceptions of how hard-line a process moderation is here and most importantly can really cut out a lot of stress for everyone. Questioning a mod decision on thread - that one catches almost everyone out because it's perfectly natural to ask what's happening and why. We need to stop sanctioning people for this and instead just split off the post(s) asking into a new thread and address it there (or via PM if it's sensitive). Punishing people for a sane and natural reaction (i.e. to ask a question and possibly express disbelief at what's happened) makes no sense at all and simply put, sends all the wrong messages. Punishing someone for asking "why?" is neither fair nor conducive to a conversation or to them learning the ropes, it just starts a fight and ends up in another closed account or over-wrought special snowflakes complaining about how the rules don't apply to the moderators friends etc.
